task_brief: This is day 5 of "Typing and Getting Organized". That is unit 3 in grade 3. Today is a mastery demonstration about organizing a simple folder. It takes about 40–60 minutes. It is one day's work, not the whole unit project. Your unit is working toward this: Create and save one clearly named, organized digital or paper folder of practice work. Today helps by working on organizing a simple folder. Your unit also covers home row typing basics, saving a file, naming files clearly, and finding a saved file. Today counts for a grade. Do it on your own.
primary_task: Show that you can do this on your own: organizing a simple folder. Put away the help sheet and the examples. Solve a new problem all the way. First write what answer you expect. Then test it two ways. Include one tricky case. Show what you expected and what you got. Then explain your thinking. Write it so someone new to organizing a simple folder could follow it. Everything you need is printed in activity_setup. It has the exact case, what should happen, how to try it, checks, and a paper choice worth the same score. Do not wait for another handout or app. Keep today's work tied to your unit. Today is about organizing a simple folder. It is part of "Typing and Getting Organized". Later days in this unit cover other things, like home row typing basics. Before you stop, do this check: Rate confidence in organizing a simple folder, cite one piece of evidence from today, and choose: ready to extend, ready to review later, or need a different explanation. In grade 3 you need one clear try with a grown-up nearby. Say or write your reason in a sentence or two. Drawings, objects, or spoken answers are all fine.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.

remediation: Reteaching for organizing a simple folder follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for organizing a simple folder, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for organizing a simple folder works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of organizing a simple folder, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking organizing a simple folder mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply organizing a simple folder under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on organizing a simple folder rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
